lessons.title: Vitamins and minerals: functions, deficiency and excess
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board — Advanced Level Food Science and Nutrition syllabus (Lower Sixth part) — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe functions of major vitamins and minerals
Describe deficiency diseases and risks of excess (in outline)
Explain bioavailability and factors affecting nutrient losses
reviewNotes: Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.
Pregnancy and supplementation statements are general only; clinical advice must come from a health worker.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Vitamins
blocks.md: **Vitamin A** (retinol; **beta-carotene** from plants such as red palm oil, carrots and leaves is converted to it): vision, epithelial tissue, immunity; deficiency: night blindness and increased infections. **Vitamin D**: calcium absorption; deficiency: rickets (children), osteomalacia (adults). **Vitamin C**: collagen formation, iron absorption; deficiency: scurvy. **B vitamins**: release of energy (B1 thiamine: beriberi; B3 niacin: pellagra); **folate**: cell division and prevention of neural tube defects in pregnancy; **B12**: only in animal foods.

blocks.title: Minerals
blocks.md: **Calcium** and **phosphorus**: bone and teeth. **Iron**: haemoglobin; deficiency: anaemia (one of the most common deficiencies). **Iodine**: thyroid hormones; deficiency: goitre and impaired development. **Zinc**: growth and immunity. **Sodium and potassium**: fluid balance, nerves, muscles. **Fluoride**: teeth.

blocks.caption: A table of five nutrients, the deficiency each causes and an example food.
blocks.alt: Table of nutrient deficiencies and foods: vitamin A night blindness, vitamin D rickets, vitamin C scurvy, iron anaemia, iodine goitre.

blocks.title: Excess and bioavailability
blocks.md: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D) can be harmful in very large doses; very high salt intake is associated with raised blood pressure. **Bioavailability** is the proportion absorbed: iron from meat is better absorbed than from plants; vitamin C increases absorption of plant iron; phytates (in whole grains and legumes) and tannins (in tea) reduce mineral absorption.

blocks.title: Losses
blocks.md: Vitamin C and B vitamins are lost by cutting, long cooking, much water, air and light. Fat-soluble vitamins are more stable but can oxidise. Steaming and quick cooking, using cooking liquid and storing food properly reduce losses.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- 'More is better' is false for fat-soluble vitamins.
- Vitamin B12 is not found in plants.
- Diagnosis of deficiency requires a health worker.
- Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Meal advice
blocks.statement: A child eats beans and green leaves with no fruit. How can iron absorption be improved at the meal?
steps: Plant iron is less well absorbed.
Add a vitamin C source such as orange or guava at the same meal.

blocks.title: Example 2 - Cooking
blocks.statement: Why is steaming better than boiling in a large pan of water for vitamin C?
steps: Vitamin C dissolves in water and is destroyed by heat.
Steaming exposes the vegetable to less water, reducing the loss.

lessons.title: Energy balance, BMR and BMI
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board — Advanced Level Food Science and Nutrition syllabus (Lower Sixth part) — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Define BMR and physical activity level
Estimate daily energy needs with a simple rule
Explain energy balance and weight change
reviewNotes: Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.
The 24 kcal/kg/day BMR rule and PAL values are rough teaching estimates; FAO/WHO prediction equations are more accurate. BMI categories are the WHO adult ones.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: BMR and activity
blocks.md: **Basal metabolic rate (BMR)** is the energy used at complete rest to keep the body alive. A simple school estimate is about **1 kcal per kg of body mass per hour** (about 24 kcal per kg per day). Total daily energy = BMR x **physical activity level (PAL)**, e.g. about 1.4 for a mostly sitting life, about 1.7 for moderate activity and about 2.0 or more for heavy work. These figures are rough and flagged for review.

blocks.title: BMI
blocks.md: **Body mass index (BMI)** = mass (kg) / height (m) squared. Adult categories used by the WHO: below 18.5 underweight; 18.5 to 24.9 healthy range; 25 to 29.9 overweight; 30 and above obese. BMI is a screening tool: it ignores muscle, age and body fat distribution; children are assessed using growth charts, not these adult cut-offs.

blocks.caption: A bar chart of the BMI limits: 18.5, 24.9 and 29.9.
blocks.alt: Bar chart of adult BMI limits used by the WHO: 18.5, 24.9 and 29.9.

blocks.title: Energy balance
blocks.md: If energy intake equals expenditure, body mass is stable. A sustained excess is stored mostly as fat; a sustained deficit causes loss of body mass. Healthy change is gradual and based on diet and activity; severe dieting is unsafe, especially for adolescents.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- BMI units: kg and metres squared (not cm).
- Applying adult BMI categories to children.
- Believing that BMR is zero when you are asleep or resting: BMR is the minimum needed.
- Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - BMI
blocks.statement: An adult has mass 70 kg and height 1.75 m. Find the BMI and category.
steps: BMI = 70 / 3.0625 = 22.9, in the 18.5 to 24.9 healthy range.

blocks.title: Example 2 - Energy estimate
blocks.statement: A 70 kg man with a mostly sitting job (PAL 1.4). Estimate daily energy (BMR rule 24 kcal/kg/day) in kcal and kJ.
steps: BMR = 70 x 24 = 1680 kcal. Total = 1680 x 1.4 = 2352 kcal.
